examDifficulty.heading: Is the Technical Architect Evaluation Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The Technical Architect Evaluation exam is very challenging. It rewards practical Salesforce experience because many questions ask you to choose the best configuration, design, or troubleshooting approach rather than recall isolated definitions.
bullets: Per exam passing score — build a margin above the minimum before booking.
Scenario-based choices — expect questions that test when to use Solution Design, Security & Identity, or Integration Architecture.
Hands-on context matters — candidates who have configured or supported Salesforce architecture in a real org are better prepared than candidates who only memorize notes.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Aim for 75%+ on timed practice sets before booking. If your score is below that, review the highest-weight topics first and retake questions until you can explain why each wrong option is wrong.

examFormat.heading: Technical Architect Evaluation Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The Technical Architect Evaluation is a Salesforce architecture assessment. Use the format below to plan preparation, design-review practice, and readiness checks.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: A meaningful share of questions are scenario-based. The common pattern is a business requirement followed by several plausible Salesforce options; your job is to identify the safest, most maintainable choice for Salesforce architecture.
bestWayToPass: Start with the official outline: Map each exam objective to your notes, Trailhead practice, and weak areas before taking full mocks.
Prioritize high-impact topics: Spend extra time on Solution Design, Security & Identity, and Integration Architecture because these usually drive the hardest scenario questions.
Practice under time pressure: Use timed question sets so you learn when to move on and return to marked questions later.
Review explanations deeply: Do not just memorize the right option; write down why the other options are less appropriate for the scenario.

certificationCard.description: The Architect Evaluation is the first step toward CTA. It assesses your ability to design secure, scalable, integrated solutions through scenario-based and multiple-choice questions. Passing this qualifies you for the Architect Review Board.

keyConcepts.h2: CTA Evaluation: Key Concepts for Success

blocks.heading: Scenario-Based Assessment Format
blocks.body: The Salesforce CTA (Certified [Technical Architect](/certifications/technical-architect)) Review Board is a scenario-based oral examination — not a multiple-choice test. Candidates receive a multi-page business scenario 30 minutes before their 2-hour board session. The scenario describes a fictional company with a complex Salesforce + external system landscape, business requirements, and technical constraints. The candidate must design a complete solution architecture, present it to a panel of 3–4 CTA evaluators, and defend it under challenge. The evaluation tests architectural thinking, communication of trade-offs, adaptability when the scenario changes, and mastery of all Salesforce platform areas.

blocks.heading: Architecture Decision Justification
blocks.body: Every architecture decision must be justified with three elements: the business requirement it satisfies, the technical reasoning (why this approach over alternatives), and the explicit trade-offs (cost, complexity, maintainability, risk). Evaluators specifically probe whether candidates can articulate why they chose X over Y — not just what they chose. Common decision areas: single org vs. multi-org, declarative vs. code, synchronous vs. async, **AppExchange** vs. custom build, Salesforce-native data store vs. external database. Preparation tip: for each major decision in practice scenarios, explicitly say "I chose X over Y because..." and name the specific trade-offs. Vague answers are probed until the candidate either justifies or concedes.

blocks.heading: Risk & Trade-off Analysis
blocks.body: CTAs are expected to proactively identify risks in their own designs — evaluators expect candidates to say "One risk with this approach is..." before being asked. Risk categories: technical risks (**governor limits**, data volume, API capacity), business risks (adoption, change management, vendor lock-in), operational risks (monitoring, support, upgrades), and security/compliance risks. Mitigation strategies must be specific — not "we will monitor it" but "we will implement a dead letter queue with alerting and a manual reprocessing workflow for failed events." Risk scoring (probability × impact) demonstrates mature architectural thinking. The evaluation rewards candidates who are intellectually honest about their design's weaknesses.

blocks.heading: Defense of Design Choices
blocks.body: The Review Board will challenge design choices with "What if..." and "Why not..." questions to test whether the candidate truly understands the solution or memorized a template. Common challenges: "What if the integration endpoint goes down for 4 hours during business hours?", "What if your MuleSoft solution is over budget — what is the fallback?", "Why didn't you use a Platform Event here instead of a REST callout?" Candidates should respond with: acknowledge the challenge, explain the impact on the current design, and either defend it (with new justification) or adapt it (with a revised approach). Changing a design under challenge is not failure — it demonstrates that the architect can think dynamically.

blocks.heading: Evaluator Rubric & Common Failure Areas
blocks.body: The CTA Review Board evaluates candidates on: Breadth (covering all required architecture areas), Depth (detailed, specific answers in each area), Communication (clear diagrams, structured verbal explanations), and Adaptability (handling scenario changes and challenges gracefully). Common failure areas: (1) Focusing only on Salesforce and ignoring external systems. (2) Providing generic answers without specific Salesforce feature references. (3) Failing to address security, data architecture, or integration explicitly. (4) Reacting defensively to challenges instead of engaging constructively. (5) Running out of time before covering all scenario requirements. Preparation: complete 10+ full mock Review Board sessions with peer CTAs or coaches, record and review yourself, and practice under time pressure.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Technical Architect Evaluation Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The CTA Evaluation program assesses your readiness for the Review Board through a structured evaluation process. Focus on demonstrating architectural breadth, clear communication, and the ability to handle ambiguous requirements.

blocks.heading: Demonstrating Architecture Breadth
blocks.body: Evaluators look for evidence of experience across all CTA domains: data architecture, integration, security, UX, environment management, and data migration. Build a portfolio of real-world architectural decisions.

blocks.heading: Handling Ambiguity
blocks.body: CTA evaluations present deliberately ambiguous scenarios. Practice asking clarifying questions, stating your assumptions clearly, and designing solutions that are flexible enough to accommodate multiple interpretations.

blocks.heading: Whiteboard Communication
blocks.body: Practice whiteboarding architecture diagrams quickly and clearly. Your diagram should show system boundaries, integration points, data flows, and key design decisions — without being cluttered.

blocks.heading: Justification Framework
blocks.body: Use a consistent framework: state the requirement, present options, identify trade-offs for each, and recommend with clear rationale. This structured approach demonstrates CTA-level thinking.

blocks.heading: Prepare with Mock Sessions
blocks.body: The CTA community regularly runs mock Review Board sessions. Participating in these is the single most effective preparation strategy — treat each mock as the real thing and seek detailed feedback.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the CTA Architect Evaluation primarily assess?
options: Scenario-based architecture design and multiple-choice technical knowledge
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Architect Evaluation is a scenario-based exam that tests your ability to design solutions and answer technical architecture questions.
whyWrong: 'Only coding skills' misrepresents the Evaluation, which assesses architecture design and technical knowledge broadly, not coding ability.
'Only presentation skills' undersells the Evaluation, which also tests scenario-based design and technical knowledge.
'Only documentation' undersells the Evaluation's actual scope, which includes technical knowledge testing too.

sampleQuestions.question: Which certifications are typically required before taking the Architect Evaluation?
options: Application Architect and System Architect (or equivalent)
sampleQuestions.explanation: Application Architect and System Architect (or equivalent) are typical prerequisites for the CTA path.
whyWrong: 'None' contradicts the fact that specific prerequisite credentials are typically required.
Platform Developer II alone doesn't provide the broad architectural foundation required.
Sales Cloud Consultant alone doesn't provide the broad architectural foundation required.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a key deliverable of the Architect Evaluation?
options: A solution design addressing the scenario requirements, constraints, and trade-offs
sampleQuestions.explanation: The evaluation requires designing a solution that addresses the scenario's requirements, constraints, and trade-offs.
whyWrong: A written essay alone doesn't capture the structured solution design deliverable the Evaluation requires.
A live coding session doesn't reflect the Evaluation's actual focus on solution design, not implementation.
A multiple-choice exam alone doesn't capture the scenario-based solution design deliverable required.

sampleQuestions.question: When designing a multi-org integration, which pattern supports data consistency?
options: Event-driven architecture with a centralized event bus
sampleQuestions.explanation: Event-driven architecture with a central bus (e.g., Platform Events, MuleSoft) supports loose coupling and consistency.
whyWrong: Point-to-point integration doesn't scale well for multi-org consistency — that's what event-driven architecture with a central bus addresses.
Synchronous REST alone doesn't provide the consistency mechanism a centralized event bus offers for multi-org scenarios.
Batch file transfer introduces latency and doesn't support the real-time consistency needs typically addressed by event-driven patterns.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary benefit of using a canonical data model in integration?
options: Reducing point-to-point mappings and simplifying maintenance across systems
sampleQuestions.explanation: Canonical models reduce coupling and simplify transformations between multiple source and target systems.
whyWrong: Faster coding isn't the benefit of a canonical data model — that benefit is about integration maintainability, not coding speed.
Lower cost alone undersells the canonical data model's core benefit around mapping simplification.
Fewer APIs isn't the specific benefit — a canonical model reduces mapping complexity, not necessarily the API count.

sampleQuestions.question: Which security consideration is critical when designing a customer-facing Community?
options: Guest user access, sharing rules, and data visibility per experience
sampleQuestions.explanation: Guest access, sharing, and profile-based visibility must be designed to protect data while enabling the right access.
whyWrong: Colors are a visual design detail, not a security consideration for guest user access.
License count alone doesn't address the specific data visibility/sharing concerns critical for guest access design.
Theme selection is a visual design detail, unrelated to data security for guest users.

sampleQuestions.question: When should you recommend Heroku vs Salesforce Platform for an application?
options: Heroku for polyglot, high-throughput, or non-Salesforce-centric workloads; Platform for CRM-centric, declarative-first
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku suits polyglot and high-scale; Platform suits CRM-centric, declarative, and Salesforce-native apps.
whyWrong: 'Always Heroku' oversimplifies the decision, which depends on workload characteristics, not a blanket rule.
'Always Platform' oversimplifies the decision, which depends on workload characteristics, not a blanket rule.
'No difference' contradicts the real, meaningful differences in fit between Heroku and the Salesforce Platform.

sampleQuestions.question: What role does the Role Hierarchy play in record-level security?
options: Users can inherit access to records owned by users below them in the hierarchy
sampleQuestions.explanation: Role hierarchy grants upward visibility: users see records owned by roles below them.
whyWrong: 'No role' contradicts the fact that role hierarchy has a defined, real impact on record-level security.
'Only for reports' undersells role hierarchy's broader record-access impact beyond just reports.
'Only for dashboards' undersells role hierarchy's broader record-access impact beyond just dashboards.

sampleQuestions.question: Which pattern supports high-volume, asynchronous integration with external systems?
options: Change Data Capture, Platform Events, or message queues
sampleQuestions.explanation: CDC, Platform Events, and queues support asynchronous, scalable integration without blocking transactions.
whyWrong: Synchronous callouts don't support the high-volume, asynchronous scenario the question specifically describes.
Workflow rules aren't designed for external system integration at volume.
Process Builder isn't designed for high-volume, asynchronous external integration.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a key trade-off when using a large data volume (LDV) strategy with Big Objects?
options: Query flexibility vs. storage and retention; Big Objects are append-only, optimized for analytics
sampleQuestions.explanation: Big Objects are append-only and optimized for analytics; they trade flexible querying for scale and retention.
whyWrong: 'No trade-offs' contradicts the fact that Big Objects involve real trade-offs between query flexibility and analytics optimization.
'Cost only' undersells the broader trade-off, which is specifically about query flexibility versus storage/retention design.
'Performance only' undersells the broader trade-off, which spans storage and retention considerations too.

sampleQuestions.question: When designing for multi-currency, what must an architect consider?
options: Advanced Currency Management, conversion dates, and reporting currency
sampleQuestions.explanation: ACM, conversion dates, and reporting currency affect accuracy and compliance in multi-currency orgs.
whyWrong: 'Only display' undersells multi-currency design, which requires backend conversion date and reporting currency configuration.
'Only manual entry' contradicts the fact that Advanced Currency Management automates conversion handling.
'Only one currency' is the opposite of what multi-currency design specifically requires.

sampleQuestions.question: Which governance practice reduces technical debt in a Salesforce org?
options: Release management, code review, and org-level standards (naming, limits)
sampleQuestions.explanation: Release management, code review, and org standards help maintain quality and reduce debt over time.
whyWrong: 'No governance' contradicts the fact that release management and standards are real governance practices that reduce technical debt.
'Only documentation' undersells governance, which spans release management and code review, not just documentation.
'Only training' undersells governance, which spans structural practices beyond just training.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the Sharing Calculator help an architect with?
options: Estimating share row counts and identifying sharing rule complexity
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Sharing Calculator estimates row-level security load and helps optimize sharing design.
whyWrong: License costs are a separate concern, not what the Sharing Calculator specifically estimates.
User count alone doesn't capture the share-row and rule-complexity estimation the Sharing Calculator provides.
Storage alone is unrelated to the Sharing Calculator's specific purpose around sharing rule impact.

sampleQuestions.question: When should an architect recommend a custom LWC over a Flow screen?
options: When complex UI, heavy logic, or reusable components are required
sampleQuestions.explanation: LWC suits complex, reusable UI; Flow suits simpler, declarative screens and guided processes.
whyWrong: 'Never' contradicts the fact that custom LWC is genuinely the right choice for certain complex scenarios.
'Always LWC' oversimplifies the decision, which depends on complexity, not a blanket rule.
'Always Flow' oversimplifies the decision — Flow isn't always sufficient for complex UI or heavy logic needs.

sampleQuestions.question: Which integration pattern supports real-time, transactional sync between Salesforce and an ERP?
options: Synchronous API (REST/SOAP) or event-driven with immediate processing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Synchronous APIs or event-driven flows with immediate handlers support real-time transactional sync.
whyWrong: 'Batch only' undersells the real-time integration patterns (synchronous API, event-driven) that support transactional ERP sync.
'File-based only' doesn't support the real-time, transactional sync the question specifically asks about.
'No real-time option' contradicts the fact that real-time integration patterns genuinely exist for this scenario.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a Solution Architecture Document (SAD)?
options: Documenting requirements, design decisions, trade-offs, and implementation approach for stakeholders
sampleQuestions.explanation: A SAD captures architecture decisions, rationale, and implementation approach for alignment and handoff.
whyWrong: 'Marketing only' misrepresents the SAD's audience and purpose, which is broader technical/business documentation.
'Only for developers' undersells the SAD's broader audience, which includes business and other stakeholders.
'Only for admins' undersells the SAD's broader audience beyond just admins.
